title: Reforming the Judiciary -- Ch. 13: A Tribute to Valedictorians
keywords: Service above self: he profits most who serves best
primary_topics: Chapter 13 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' -- CJP's April 6, 2002 address to the Rotary Club of Downtown Manila's 'Tribute to Valedictorians,' arguing that 'academic excellence, by itself, is not enough' and must be supplemented by three other traits, the three Ps of patience, perseverance and prayer.

His identification with the scholarship recipients through his own impoverished boyhood -- hawking newspapers, shining shoes and peddling cigarettes in Sampaloc -- and his admission, in Filipino, that he himself was only an honor graduate and not a valedictorian.

Patience as the virtue brilliant people most lack: his warning that gifted individuals grow impetuous, overbearing and dismissive of others, illustrated by his own youthful impatience and by the analogy of reckless overspeeding.

Perseverance and prayer as the remaining two Ps -- hard work over bare talent, faith that God answers 'in His own way, not our way; in His own time, not at the time we demand,' and a daily habit of prayer in whatever language and length.
sub_topics: He praises the Rotary Club of Downtown Manila under President Arsenio S. Ong for sponsoring the tribute and granting college scholarships, calling it a demonstration of the Rotary motto 'Service above self: he profits most who serves best.'
He congratulates the valedictorians, parents, principals, teachers and the 600 Rotarians present for proclaiming their faith in academic excellence as the key to success.
He recalls his own graduation from Mapa High School some 45 years earlier, and a father who was a poor but honest government employee providing for four children and seven siblings.

He recounts hawking newspapers, shining shoes and peddling cigarettes on the sidewalks of Espana and Cataluna Streets, and selling bibles to his teachers and textbooks to his classmates so he could keep copies himself.

He says that although he has achieved 'the dream of every lawyer' -- a seat on the Supreme Court -- he still identifies with the graduates and is even envious, since 'Honor graduate lang po ako, hindi valedictorian.'
Switching to Filipino, he tells them their intelligence is a blessing from the Maykapal and the capital with which they will build a good future, and that if he could succeed, so can they.

First P -- patience: brilliant people become maladjusted because they are in a hurry, becoming impetuous and reckless, presuming everyone else is bright, failing to explain themselves, and ending up regarded as mayabang or mataray.

He admits that when young he was always in a hurry, demanded the same of everyone, grew angry when they could not measure up, and so had difficulty relating to people; he likens haste to overspeeding and advises tolerance of contrary opinions and to 'make haste slowly.'

Second P -- perseverance: he cites Thomas Edison's motto that genius is ninety-nine percent perspiration, and Diosdado Banatao, the successful Filipino entrepreneur in California who told Asiaweek his secret was hard work and that 'For every success, there are 100 or 200 failures.'

He recites the ladder of failures -- business collapse, lost legislative, congressional, senatorial and vice-presidential races, a nervous breakdown, the death of a sweetheart -- before revealing the man as Abraham Lincoln, elected President at sixty.

He tells the Middle Ages story of the farmer whose lost horse, ten returned horses, injured son and spared conscription each drew the same reply: 'Good luck? Bad luck? Who knows? I will just keep doing my best,' urging the graduates to meet uncontrollable events the same way.

Third P -- prayer: believe in a God more powerful than all of us, who knows our needs better than we do and answers in His own time and way, quoting Isaiah that 'My thoughts are not your thoughts, and my ways are not your ways.'
He assures them that God has never abandoned him in his struggles and will not forget them, and that even in prayer 'we must be patient and persevering.'

He notes that the Supreme Court and all other courts, the Senate, the House and the Cabinet open their sessions with prayer, and recommends beginning each day with one -- memorized or homemade, in English, Tagalog or any dialect, a minute or an hour, so long as it is sincere.

In the epilogue he asks them to remember the three Ps when college brings new challenges, and imagines them decades later telling their children that they heard and practiced patience, perseverance and prayer at this April 6, 2002 tribute.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 13 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' reproduced CJP's April 6, 2002 address to the Rotary Club of Downtown Manila's 'Tribute to Valedictorians,' a gathering of 600 Rotarians honoring high school valedictorians from Metropolitan Manila and granting them college scholarships. He praised the club under President Arsenio S. Ong as a demonstration of the Rotary motto 'Service above self: he profits most who serves best,' then identified himself with the honorees by recalling his own graduation from Mapa High School some 45 years earlier, a poor but honest government-employee father supporting four children and seven siblings, and his own hawking of newspapers, shining of shoes and peddling of cigarettes on the sidewalks of Espana and Cataluna Streets, along with selling bibles to teachers and textbooks to classmates. Though he had reached 'the dream of every lawyer' in the Supreme Court, he told them he envied them, since 'Honor graduate lang po ako, hindi valedictorian.' His thesis was that 'academic excellence, by itself, is not enough': it must be joined to three other traits, the three Ps. On patience, he warned that brilliant people become impetuous, overbearing and dismissive, confessed that he himself had always been in a hurry and had grown angry when others could not keep up, likened haste to overspeeding, and advised his listeners to 'make haste slowly.' On perseverance, he cited Edison's motto on perspiration, the entrepreneur Diosdado Banatao's report to Asiaweek that 'For every success, there are 100 or 200 failures,' the long chain of defeats that preceded Abraham Lincoln's election at sixty, and the medieval parable of the farmer whose every turn of fortune drew the reply 'Good luck? Bad luck? Who knows? I will just keep doing my best,' concluding that adversities are often preludes to greater victory. On prayer, he quoted Isaiah on God's higher thoughts and ways, testified that God had never abandoned him, noted that the courts, Senate, House and Cabinet all open with prayer, and urged a daily, sincere prayer of any length or language, since God answers 'in His own way, not our way; in His own time, not at the time we demand.'
